stem: U(x,y)=x+y and px+y=10. At p=1/2, what is the absolute own-price elasticity of demand for x?
solution: Since p<1, x gives more utility per rupee, so the consumer spends all income on x: x=10/p. Differentiation gives signed elasticity (−10/p²)(p/(10/p))=−1, absolute value1.
hint: Identify which perfect substitute is cheaper.

stem:
Good x costs p locally and q

C. Good y costs1 everywhere. For smooth downward-sloping convex indifference curves, if optimal x is x₀, which statement holds?
answer: C is possible under the literal assumptions: (p−q)x₀=C may hold at a corner but cannot hold at an interior crossing.
solution: The local and distant budget lines are y=I−px and y=I−C−qx; they meet at x*=C/(p−q). At an interior crossing, the upper budget envelope has a slope increase from −p to−q. Smooth monotone utility cannot have a local maximum there: its derivative along the right branch exceeds that along the left by(p−q)U_y>0. Thus equality is impossible for an interior optimum, the likely intended answerB. However, the source permits corner optima. Take p=2,q=1,C=1,I=2 and U=x+0.1log(1+y). Its smooth strictly convex indifference curves meet both budget lines optimally at(x,y)=(1,0), satisfying(p−q)x=C. Other preferences at the same prices choose a different bundle. Therefore the literal question admits optionC; an interiority assumption is needed to assertB.
hint: Inspect the crossing of the two budget lines, including its endpoints.
notes: Corner counterexample prevents the usual interior-only answer from being universal; no automatic grading.
options: Equality may or may not hold depending on preferences

stem: For Q=min(L/(2a),K/(4b)), with a,b>0 and factor prices w,r, what is the cost function?
solution: Output Q requires at least L=2aQ and K=4bQ. With positive input prices, these minima are chosen, so cost is2awQ+4brQ. None of the first three options equals this expression.

stem: An economy has positive net borrowing from abroad during a period. Under the standard net-borrowing/current-account identity, what follows?
solution: Net foreign borrowing finances a current-account deficit: current account equals national saving minus investment, while net borrowing is investment minus saving. Thus positive net borrowing implies negative current account. It does not separately determine trade balance, net factor income or reserve changes. A positive particular loan inflow alone, as opposed to net foreign borrowing across all financial flows, would not suffice for this inference.
notes: “Net loan from abroad” is read as total net foreign borrowing, not just one loan flow.
options: Net factor income from abroad is negative

stem: In a simple Keynesian economy G=tY always balances total income-tax receipts. What happens to Y if government raises t?
answer: A: Y increases under the usual proportional-consumption, exogenous-investment assumptions.
solution: Let C=c(1−t)Y,0<c<1, and investment I>0 be fixed. Then Y=C+I+G gives Y=I/[(1−c)(1−t)], increasing in t for0≤t<1. Shifting one rupee from private disposable income to government spending raises expenditure because government spends the full rupee while households would have spent only c of it.
notes: Uses the standard simple-Keynesian proportional-consumption and fixed-investment setup implicit in the question.

stem: Which statement is false? Under the conventional textbook treatment of public-debt interest, it is not a part of…
answer: D: “personal income” is the false exclusion.
solution: Public-debt interest received by households contributes to personal income. In the textbook transfer-payment treatment used by this question, it is excluded from national income generated by current production and is not government consumption expenditure. Hence denying its inclusion in personal income is false. OptionA is read as saying it is not included in both income aggregates simultaneously; if instead “not part of both” means excluded from each, that wording is ambiguous.
hint: Distinguish household receipts from income generated by current production.
notes: Uses the source’s conventional public-interest-as-transfer classification; optionA has a scope ambiguity in ordinary language.
options: Both personal income and national income

stem: Explain true/false: (i) Fixed gallons of gasoline per barrel of crude imply a gasoline/crude price ratio independent of crude production. (ii) Without money illusion, all price elasticities of a commodity determine its income elasticity. (iii) If both people have homothetic preferences, an Edgeworth-box contract curve is the straight line between origins.
answer: (i) False in general. (ii) True under differentiable degree-zero homogeneous demand. (iii) False.
solution: (i) A fixed physical conversion coefficient does not determine market prices. With yield a and extra processing cost c per barrel, competitive gasoline price is(p_crude+c)/a, whose ratio to crude price is1/a+c/(a p_crude), varying when crude scarcity changes its price. (ii) No money illusion means xᵢ(λp,λM)=xᵢ(p,M). Euler’s theorem yields Σⱼpⱼ∂xᵢ/∂pⱼ+M∂xᵢ/∂M=0. Dividing by xᵢ gives income elasticity ηᵢ=−Σⱼεᵢⱼ. (iii) Different homothetic preferences need not have the same MRS along the diagonal. For totals(1,1), take U_A=√(xy) and U_B=x^(1/4)y^(3/4). Tangency yields y_A=x_A/(3−2x_A), a curved contract curve, not the diagonal.
hint: Distinguish technology from pricing and apply homogeneity to demand.

stem: Duopoly demand is P=10−q₁−q₂. For positive output, costs are C₁=1+2q₁ and C₂=1+4q₂; a firm producing nothing avoids its fixed cost. Find Cournot outputs and profits. What if firm2 fixed cost rises from1 to2?
answer: Initially q₁=10/3,q₂=4/3, profits91/9 and7/9. After firm2 fixed cost becomes2, equilibrium is q₁=4,q₂=0, profits15 and0.
solution: Conditional on producing, first-order conditions are2q₁+q₂=8 and q₁+2q₂=6. They give(10/3,4/3). At each optimum operating profit equals qᵢ², so subtracting fixed cost1 gives91/9 and7/9, both positive. Raising firm2 fixed cost to2 makes its former net profit16/9−2=−2/9, so that interior solution is not an equilibrium. If firm2 exits, firm1 optimally chooses monopoly output4 and earns(10−4−2)4−1=15. Against q₁=4, firm2’s best positive output is1, with operating profit1<fixed cost2, so staying out is optimal. Thus(4,0) is the new equilibrium.
hint: Check shutdown as well as the positive-output first-order conditions.

stem: Group1 income is fixed800; its propensity to consume is.8 and propensity to import.4. Group2 consumes only domestic output with propensity.5. Investment is domestically produced and fixed600. (i) Find GDP. (ii) Group2 transfers100 to group1 and imports are capped250: find new GDP. (iii) Repeat with import cap400.
answer: Initial Y1040. After transfer with cap250, Y1240 (rise200). With cap400, Y1020 (fall20 from initial).
solution: Initially C₁=.8·800=640, C₂=.5(Y−800), imports=.4·800=320. Goods balance Y=C₁+C₂+600−320 gives Y1040. After transfer, disposable incomes are900 andY−900. C₁=720 and C₂=.5(Y−900). Desired imports360 exceed cap250, so Y=720+.5(Y−900)+600−250, yielding1240. With cap400, imports360 are not constrained, so the same balance with−360 yields1020. The transfer changes consumption patterns but is not itself new GDP; the import cap changes the domestic share of spending.
hint: Track each group’s disposable income and subtract actual, capped imports.

stem: A consumer buys electricity E and other goods O priced1. Electricity requires fixed charge R and a quantity-dependent per-unit price p=E/2. Utility is E+O and income I>R. (i) Describe the budget boundary. (ii) For R0,I1 find the optimum. (iii) Find the largest extractable fixed charge.
answer: Reading p as the price applied to all units: O=I−R−E²/2 when connected. At R0,I1: E1,O1/2. At I1 the maximal fixed charge is1/2, leaving the consumer indifferent to no connection.
solution: With an all-units price p(E), total electricity spending is p(E)E=E²/2. Thus the connected budget is a downward parabola O=I−R−E²/2 for0<E≤√[2(I−R)], together with the no-connection option E0,O≤I if the fee is avoidable. For R0,I1, utility along the parabola is1+E−E²/2, uniquely maximized at E1,O1/2. The maximal gross surplus from access is max(E−E²/2)=1/2, so at I1 a charge R1/2 extracts it: E1,O0,U1 equals no-connection utility1. A charge just below1/2 ensures strict participation. More generally, with no borrowing and income I, R_max=1/2 if I≥1; for0<I<1 the affordability constraint yields R_max=I−I²/2 at E=I,O0. If p were intended as a marginal-block tariff, total spending would instead be E²/4 and the numerical answers would differ; the all-units interpretation is the literal per-unit-price reading.
hint: The total bill is quantity times the all-units price, plus the connection fee.
notes: The price function is interpreted as an all-units price rather than a marginal tariff; the continuation of I1 is used for the main fixed-charge answer.

stem: Income is25, prices are3 for x and4 for y, and U=12x+16y−x²−y² on x,y≥0. What happens to the optimum if income rises to50 or more?
answer: At income25, bundle(3,4). At income50 or more, bundle(6,8); any income above50 is left unspent.
solution: Complete squares: U=100−(x−6)²−(y−8)². The unconstrained bliss point is(6,8), costing3·6+4·8=50. With income25, the closest feasible point to that bliss point lies on3x+4y25 and equals(6,8)−(3,4)=(3,4). At income50 the bliss point becomes affordable and maximizes utility100. Further income cannot improve on satiation, so the same bundle remains optimal with unspent income.
hint: Locate the bliss point by completing squares.

stem: IS–LM has desired private saving s=s(Y−tθY),0<s′<1; investment i=i(r),i′<0; money demand l(Y,r) with l_Y>0,l_r<0. Labour share θ, real money M/P, G and tax rate t are exogenous. (i) Can equilibrium tax collections tθY fall when t rises? (ii) If tax instead applies to all GNP, reformulate saving and reconsider.
answer: Under these assumptions equilibrium tax revenue strictly increases with t; no downward Laffer segment occurs. Replacing labour taxation by all-income taxation sets θ1 and leaves that conclusion intact.
solution: Goods equilibrium is s((1−θt)Y)+θtY=i(r)+G, because private plus government saving equals investment. Along fixed-money LM, dr=k dY with k=−l_Y/l_r>0. Let a=s′ and D=a(1−θt)+θt−i′k>0. Differentiating gives dY/dt=−θY(1−a)/D<0. Revenue R=θtY has derivative dR/dt=θY[1−θt(1−a)/D]=θY(a−i′k)/D>0. Thus the negative income response never outweighs the direct rate effect in this model. If all income is taxed, saving becomes s((1−t)Y), tax revenue is tY and the same derivation with θ1 gives positive derivative Y(a−i′k)/[a(1−t)+t−i′k]. Therefore extending the tax base does not introduce a downward-sloping Laffer branch under these behavioural restrictions.
hint: Include government saving, differentiate both equilibrium conditions and then differentiate tax revenue.
notes: Assumes positive income, 0<θ≤1 and economically admissible tax rates0≤t<1.
